title: End of Year Value Booster: Ask Them
author: Dave Stuart Jr.
summary: Following up on a companion piece about teacher-delivered mini-sermons, Stuart argues that student-generated value statements are actually the stronger motivational lever, and this article gives the exact warm-up he uses to produce them. Students respond in writing to a devil's-advocate prompt — imagine you had to justify to a younger student why all the semester's work "was worth it," without falling back on "I needed to pass the class" — while the teacher circulates and publicly highlights the strongest arguments. He frames it as harder for demotivated students, so he builds in a villain-framing device to lower the stakes and make the task feel like a game rather than a sincere confession. The activity closes with a Pair-Share and a direct callback: the teacher tells students that although this class is ending, they've just practiced a skill their most important future teacher — themselves — will keep needing. It's presented as a low-cost, high-leverage way to end a course by putting the burden of meaning-making on students rather than the teacher.
points: Distinguishes teacher-generated Value signals (mini-sermons) from student-generated ones, and argues the latter are the stronger, first-best lever per The Will to Learn.
Supplies an exact writing prompt with a built-in constraint (can't just say "I needed to pass") that forces students past the easiest, least meaningful answer.
Uses a "villain" framing device specifically to lower the emotional stakes for demotivated students who would otherwise struggle to engage honestly with the prompt.
Closes with a direct reframing move — telling students their most important future teacher is themselves — that ties a single warm-up activity to a lifelong disposition.
quotes: BUT as I argue in The Will to Learn, teacher-generated Value signals are actually the second-best approach to cultivating Value in the secondary classroom. The first-best are student-generated Value signals.
So let's pretend that in order to pass this class, you had to explain to a younger student why all this work was worth it. Why, to you, does this matter? What was all this work for?
Now for a warning: your demotivated students are going to have a hard time with this. You can help them by framing it as a devil's advocate sort of activity.
To help your students, walk around while they're writing, looking over their shoulders for any decent arguments. As you see them, call them out.
In a few weeks, this class will be over. My time as your teacher will be through. But the most important teacher you'll ever have will still be with you: you.
